title: Query Client
description: Deep dive into the QueryClient and its methods for managing cache and queries.

data.text: The **QueryClient** is the central engine of React Query. It holds the cache, runs queries, and exposes imperative methods for cache manipulation. Most of the time you interact with it indirectly through hooks, but understanding the QueryClient unlocks advanced patterns like optimistic updates and manual cache management.
Inside a React component, use the useQueryClient hook to get a reference to the QueryClient instance. This is the most common way to interact with the cache programmatically.

data.title: useQueryClient Hook
data.content: Accessing the QueryClient from within a component

data.text: The QueryClient exposes methods for reading, writing, and invalidating cached data. Here are the most commonly used methods:

rows: Read cached users to show in a tooltip
Write or update cached data directly
Mark queries as stale, trigger refetch
After a mutation, refetch the affected list
Find all cached data matching a filter
Bulk update after a bulk mutation

data.text: getQueryData lets you read data from the cache synchronously without triggering a network request. It returns undefined if the data is not in the cache or has been garbage-collected.

data.title: getQueryData â€” Read from Cache
data.content: Reading cached users without triggering a fetch

data.text: setQueryData lets you write data directly to the cache. Use it for optimistic updates â€” updating the UI before the server confirms the change. The update function receives the previous cached value and must return the new value.

data.title: setQueryData â€” Optimistic Update
data.content: Updating cache after a mutation without waiting for refetch

data.text: invalidateQueries marks matching queries as stale and triggers a refetch. This is the standard way to refresh data after a mutation. React Query's default behavior is to refetch stale queries when the window regains focus, so invalidation keeps data fresh without manual polling.

data.caption: How invalidateQueries triggers a refetch cycle
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Mutation
    participant QC as QueryClient
    participant C as Component
    participant S as Server
    M->>QC: invalidateQueries(['users'])
    QC->>QC: Mark 'users' query as stale
    QC->>C: Notify subscribers of change
    C->>QC: useQuery sees stale data
    QC->>S: Refetch /api/users
    S-->>QC: Return fresh data
    QC->>QC: Update cache
    QC->>C: Re-render with fresh data

data.title: invalidateQueries After Mutation
data.content: Refreshing the users list after adding a new user

data.text: refetchQueries forces an immediate refetch regardless of the staleTime setting. Use this for manual refresh buttons where the user explicitly wants fresh data.

data.title: refetchQueries â€” Manual Refresh
data.content: Forcing a refetch on user action

data.title: invalidateQueries vs refetchQueries
data.text: Use invalidateQueries after mutations â€” it marks data as stale and respects your staleTime/gcTime settings. Use refetchQueries only for explicit user-triggered refreshes where you want to bypass staleTime.

Query keys are arrays that identify queries in the cache. React Query supports hierarchical keys: invalidating ['users'] also invalidates ['users', 1] and ['users', 'filtered']. This is one of the most powerful features of the library.

data.title: Query Key Patterns
items: ['posts', postId, 'comments'] â€” comments for a specific post

terms.definition: A unique array identifier for a query in the React Query cache. All parts of the array are used for matching â€” invalidating ['users'] also invalidates ['users', 1].
Marking cached data as stale so that React Query will refetch it on the next relevant render or window focus event.
Updating the cache immediately after a mutation before the server responds, so the UI feels instant. If the server fails, roll back the change.

data.title: Manual Cache Manipulation
data.description: Build a simple todo list app that uses React Query's QueryClient methods directly. Practice getQueryData, setQueryData, and invalidateQueries without relying solely on hooks.
steps: Set up a React app with QueryClientProvider using the configuration from the Setup lesson
Create a fetchTodos function that returns a Promise resolving to an array of todos
Use useQuery to load the initial todo list with queryKey ['todos']
Add a button that calls queryClient.getQueryData(['todos']) and logs the result
Add a button that calls queryClient.setQueryData to prepend a new todo without a network request
Add a form that uses useMutation to POST a new todo, then calls invalidateQueries(['todos']) in onSuccess
Verify that setQueryData updates the UI instantly, and invalidateQueries refreshes the list from the server
data.expectedOutcome: A working todo list where you can read the cache directly, optimistically add items, and see the list refresh after a successful mutation. Console logs confirm each QueryClient method was called correctly.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: QueryClient is the central cache manager for React Query
Use useQueryClient hook inside components to access it
getQueryData reads cache without triggering a fetch
setQueryData writes cache directly â€” great for optimistic updates
invalidateQueries marks data as stale and triggers refetch
refetchQueries forces an immediate refetch regardless of staleTime
Query keys are hierarchical â€” invalidating a parent key invalidates all children
data.takeaway: The QueryClient gives you imperative control over the cache when hooks alone are not enough.
